openingMessage: The price of success is hard work, dedication to the job at hand, and the determination that whether we win or lose, we have applied the best of ourselves to the task.
openingWhy: Some days the well wins anyway — weather, downhole, plain luck. What can't ever happen is the well winning because we showed up loose. Rained out and rescheduled with the standard intact is a good day. Finished early with steps skipped is a loss, whatever the ticket says.
leadershipThought: Recognition is culture in action. When you name what someone did right, you tell the whole crew what right looks like. Kudos to the ones doing it right every day.

Man basket work is one of the highest-risk lift operations on an oil and gas site — Stop Work Authority before elevation is always the right call when anything about the setup looks wrong.

Positive Observation — LOTO Disconnect Completed Efficiently (Energy Isolation)
LOTO, atmospheric testing, and hold points together form a complete energy control system — don't shortcut any one of them, even on a quick job.

Stop Work by Equipment Operator — Spotter Lost Visual (Mobile Equipment)
Equipment operators own Stop Work Authority too — stop the moment you lose your spotter; regaining visual contact is the only acceptable restart condition.

Crane Work — Horse Head Installation and Flowline Connection (Mobile Equipment)
Crane work demands real-time stop work authority — if anything changes during the lift, the person on the ground is empowered to call the stop immediately.

specialFocus.title: Confined Space — Activate the Permit. Log the Air.
specialFocus.why: This section exists because of a real accusation against our group: a claim that a permit wasn't activated before a job — on work our crew did right, with every piece of paperwork filled out. The documentation is what won that argument. That is the lesson, and it only has to be learned once: doing it right is not enough on its own — the record has to prove it, to the minute. From today forward this is how Canon runs every confined space job. We have confined space work on the board — this applies before anyone breaks the plane.
standard: No entry — ever — without a pre-entry permit that is ACTIVATED before anyone breaks the plane. Filled out is not activated. A permit is live when it is authorized, signed, and time-stamped, before the job starts.

Atmospheric testing goes in the log, in writing: initial readings with the time and the tester's name before entry, then continuous or periodic readings recorded through the job. Every reading gets a timestamp.
The permit and the air log ride together and get retained after the job. If it isn't written down with a time on it, you cannot prove it happened — and someday you may have to.
specialFocus.scenario: A crew runs a textbook entry: JSA done, permit filled out, gas tests taken, job goes clean. Days later an accusation lands — 'the permit was never activated before the job.' Memory won't settle it. Word against word won't settle it. The only thing that settles it is the paper: an authorization signature with a time on it, and an atmospheric log whose first readings are stamped BEFORE the entry time. If your permit shows activation at 08:42 and your first readings at 08:35, the accusation dies in thirty seconds. If your paperwork is perfect except that one line — you did the job right and you still can't prove it.
questions: On your last confined space entry — could your paperwork prove, to the minute, that the permit was activated and the air was tested before anyone went in? Who signed it, and when?
What is the difference between a permit that is filled out and a permit that is activated? Who makes ours live, and what exactly makes it live?
If someone accuses this crew tomorrow of skipping a step you actually did — which document saves you, and is it filled out that way today?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: There is no version of this job where we enter first and paper up after. Permit activated. Air tested and logged. Then entry. Every time. This is not optional.
